title: repairs
text:
Some mistakes in a reading cannot be fixed by rule. A person has to look at the scan, decide what the page really says, and write that decision down. The functions here apply those decisions, along with a few repairs that need a hint from you, such as where a chapter starts.
Most of them work on pages of blocks, [{page, blocks}] (or items), before assemble puts the verses into chapters. A block is one piece of a page as the vision model read it: a verse, a heading, a colophon (the line that closes a chapter), a commentary or prose. These functions change the pages in place and also return them. fix_chapters and sutras work later, on the chapters assemble returns. Every change goes into probs, a list you pass in, so the list of problems also says what was changed and why.
They were written for books vedicreader read and had to repair again and again: the fix tables for the Bṛhat Saṃhitā, the Muhūrta Cintāmaṇi and the Nārada Saṃhitā, the unnumbered runs of the Phaladīpikā, the second readings of the Jātaka Pārijāta, and the chapter plans of the Grahacintāmaṇi.

title: repairs
text:
A table of fixes
Each correction is a fix row, (page, item, kind, read, printed, why). page and item say where the mistake is: the page’s name and the block’s position on that page, counting from 0. read is the text as the model read it, printed is what the page prints, and why is your reason, which goes into probs with the change. kind says what to do:

fix replaces the first occurrence of read in the block’s text with printed, and fix_all replaces every occurrence.
doubt is a fix you are not sure of. It is applied only when witness, a dict keyed by (page, item, read), holds 'agrees' for it, meaning another edition reads the same way. Otherwise the text is kept and the doubt is recorded.
slip records a mistake that the printed book itself makes. The text is kept, since it matches the print.
number sets the block’s number to printed.
drop removes the block.
missing adds a block the model skipped. printed is the whole block as a dict, and it goes in after position item, or first on the page when item is -1.

Blocks are removed and added only after every row has been read, so the positions in all the rows refer to the page as the model read it. A row for a page that is not in the reading is ignored. A row whose position is past the end of the page, or whose read text is not in the block, is not applied, and that is recorded in probs. The test below applies rows of several kinds to one small page.


source

apply_fixes
def apply_fixes(
    pages, rows, witness:dict=None, probs:list=None
)->list:
Apply a table of fix rows (page, item, kind, read, printed, why) to pages of blocks, recording each change in probs.



_pg = lambda: [dict(page='p1', blocks=[dict(kind='verse', n=1, text='रामः वनं गच्छति ॥१॥'), dict(kind='verse', n=3, text='सीता ॥३॥'), dict(kind='prose', text='a note')])]
_p = []
_r = apply_fixes(_pg(), [('p1', 0, 'fix', 'गच्छति', 'गच्छत्', 'the print'), ('p1', 1, 'number', 3, 2, ''), ('p1', 2, 'drop', None, None, 'a footnote'),
                         ('p1', 1, 'missing', None, dict(kind='verse', n=3, text='लक्ष्मणः ॥३॥'), 'at the foot'), ('p1', 0, 'doubt', 'रामः', 'राम', 'faint')], probs=_p)
test_eq([(b['n'], b['text']) for b in _r[0]['blocks']], [(1, 'रामः वनं गच्छत् ॥१॥'), (2, 'सीता ॥३॥'), (3, 'लक्ष्मणः ॥३॥')])
test_eq(len(_p), 5); assert any('doubt' in x for x in _p)
test_eq(apply_fixes(_pg(), [('p1', 0, 'doubt', 'रामः', 'राम', '')], witness={('p1', 0, 'रामः'): 'agrees'})[0]['blocks'][0]['text'][:3], 'राम')
_p = []; test_eq(apply_fixes([dict(page=0, blocks=[dict(kind='verse', text='क क ख')])], [(0, 0, 'fix_all', 'क', 'ग', '')], probs=_p)[0]['blocks'][0]['text'], 'ग ग ख')
test_eq(_p, ['0: read `क`, printed `ग`, 2 times'])

title: repairs
text:
Numbers
Models often miss a verse number, especially one printed small or faint, or at the edge of the page. Two functions recover such numbers without asking a person.
If verse 4 follows verse 1 with two unnumbered verse blocks between them, those two must be verses 2 and 3. number_runs numbers a run of unnumbered verses when it exactly fills the gap between two numbered ones, and leaves it alone otherwise. Only blocks of kind verse count. The count starts again from 0 after a colophon, and after a heading that matches reset (ध्याय by default, as in अध्यायः), so the first verses of a new chapter can be numbered from 1.
borrow_numbers uses a second reading of the same pages, by another model or another run. For each unnumbered verse, it finds the most similar numbered verse on the same page of the other reading and takes its number, if the two texts are at least at alike (0.6 by default, where 1 means identical) and no verse on this page already has that number.


source

borrow_numbers
def borrow_numbers(
    pages, other, probs:list=None, at:float=0.6
)->list:
Give each unnumbered verse the number of the most similar verse on the same page of other, a second reading of the same pages.




source

number_runs
def number_runs(
    pages, probs:list=None, reset:str='ध्याय'
)->list:
Number each run of unnumbered verses that exactly fills the gap between two numbered ones.



_ps = [dict(page=0, blocks=[dict(kind='verse', n=1, text='a'), dict(kind='verse', text='b'), dict(kind='verse', text='c'), dict(kind='verse', n=4, text='d'),
                             dict(kind='colophon', text='इति'), dict(kind='verse', text='e'), dict(kind='verse', n=3, text='f')])]
test_eq([b.get('n') for b in number_runs(_ps)[0]['blocks']], [1, 2, 3, 4, None, None, 3])   # after the colophon one verse cannot fill 1..2
_mine = [dict(page=0, blocks=[dict(kind='verse', text='धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे'), dict(kind='verse', n=2, text='दृष्ट्वा तु')])]
_theirs = [dict(page=0, blocks=[dict(kind='verse', n='१', text='धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता'), dict(kind='verse', n='२', text='दृष्ट्वा तु')])]
test_eq([b['n'] for b in borrow_numbers(_mine, _theirs)[0]['blocks']], [1, 2])


_it = [dict(page=0, items=[dict(kind='verse', n=1, text='a'), dict(kind='verse', text='b'), dict(kind='head', text='द्वितीयोऽध्यायः'), dict(kind='verse', text='c'), dict(kind='verse', n=2, text='d')])]
test_eq([b.get('n') for b in number_runs(_it)[0]['items']], [1, None, None, 1, 2])   # `items` read as blocks, a `head` as a heading
test_eq([b['n'] for b in borrow_numbers([dict(page=0, items=[dict(kind='verse', text='धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे')])], _theirs)[0]['items']], [1])
test_eq(len(apply_fixes([dict(page=0, items=[dict(kind='verse', text='x')])], [(0, 0, 'drop', None, None, '')])[0]['items']), 0)

title: repairs
text:
Chapters by plan
Some books start a chapter in a way assemble cannot see: with a heading the model did not mark as one, or with no mark at all because a leaf is missing. cut_by_plan takes a plan, a list of (page, item, why) rows saying where each such chapter begins. item is either a block’s position on the page or the first words of a block’s text, usually a heading, and why is optional. Before that block it puts a block of kind start, and assemble begins a new chapter at a start block. Each cut is recorded in probs, and so is a row whose page or block cannot be found.


source

cut_by_plan
def cut_by_plan(
    pages, plan, probs:list=None
)->list:
Insert a chapter-opening start block at each (page, item, why) row of plan, where item is a block’s position or the first words of its text.



from lekhaka.verses import assemble
_pl = [dict(page=0, blocks=[dict(kind='heading', text='கடவுள் வணக்கம்'), dict(kind='verse', n=1, text='x'), dict(kind='heading', text='வாரநயம்'), dict(kind='verse', n=2, text='y')])]
_p = []; _c, _ = assemble(cut_by_plan(_pl, [(0, 'வாரநயம்')], _p)); test_eq(_p, ['0: a chapter starts at `வாரநயம்`, by the plan'])
test_eq([(c['heading'], c['colophon'], [v['n'] for v in c['verses']]) for c in _c], [('கடவுள் வணக்கம்', None, [1]), ('வாரநயம்', None, [2])])
_p = []; cut_by_plan(_pl, [(5, 0), (0, 'அது')], _p); test_eq(len(_p), 2)
_p = []; cut_by_plan([dict(page='p2', items=[dict(kind='verse', n='२', text='x')])], [('p2', 0, 'the leaf before it lost')], _p)
test_eq(_p, ['p2: a chapter starts at verse 2, by the plan (the leaf before it lost)'])

title: repairs
section: Pages that are not the text
text:
Pages that are not the text
Printed books often carry pages whose verses are not part of the work, such as a preface, an index, or an appendix quoting another work. The Phaladīpikā edition, for example, prints verses of the Jātakābharaṇa after verse 26.48. drop_pages takes a list of (first, last) page ranges, both ends included, and removes the verse blocks on those pages. Headings and other blocks stay.


source

drop_pages
def drop_pages(
    pages, ranges, probs:list=None
)->list:
Remove the verse blocks on every page in each (first, last) range, for pages that are not part of the text.



_p = []
_d = drop_pages([dict(page=k, items=[dict(kind='heading', text='h'), dict(kind='verse', n=k, text='v')]) for k in range(1, 5)], [(2, 3)], _p)
test_eq([len(p['items']) for p in _d], [2, 1, 1, 2]); test_eq(_p, ['2: verses dropped, not the text', '3: verses dropped, not the text'])

title: repairs
text:
After assembly
Once assemble has built the chapters, it is easier to name a verse by its chapter and number than by its page and position. fix_chapters takes fix rows (chapter, verse, kind, read, printed, why), where verse is the verse’s number. chapter is the chapter’s position counting from 1, unless you pass key, a function key(i, chapter) that names chapters some other way, such as the edition’s own chapter numbers or a (part, no) pair. A chapter of None applies the row to every chapter that has that verse. The rows are applied in order, so after a start row has split a chapter, the rows that follow count the chapters as split.
The kinds are:

fix and fix_all replace read with printed in the verse, once or every time, as in apply_fixes.
slip and doubt are recorded and the text is kept. A doubt is never applied here, since fix_chapters takes no witness.
note records why as a remark on the verse and changes nothing.
number sets the verse’s number to printed, and drop removes the verse.
missing adds a verse the reading lacks, perhaps copied by hand from another copy of the book. printed is its text, or a dict such as {text, page}, and it goes in at its place by number. If the chapter already has a verse with that number, nothing is added.
recut moves the boundary between a verse and the one before it, for a case mend cannot see, such as a four-line verse whose last line has no daṇḍa, so the model ran it into the next verse. The two verses are joined and split again so that the earlier one keeps the first printed lines.
start begins a new chapter at the verse. This is for a lost leaf that took the end of one chapter and the start of the next, so the numbering does not restart where assemble would notice. The verse cannot be the first of its chapter. If a chapter holds two verses with that number, printed says which one: the page it is on, or 1 for the first and 2 for the second. The first part keeps the chapter’s heading and the second keeps its colophon.

Any other kind raises a ValueError.
sutras is for works written in sūtras, short prose aphorisms, rather than verse. It puts each sūtra on one line, joining wrapped lines and removing a hyphen at a line break. Where a sūtra does not end in close (॥ by default), it removes a final । or | and adds close, recording that in probs.


source

sutras
def sutras(
    chs, probs:list=None, close:str='॥', key:NoneType=None
)->list:
Put each sūtra on one line, rejoining words hyphenated at a line break, and end it with close where the reading lost it.




source

fix_chapters
def fix_chapters(
    chs, rows, probs:list=None, key:NoneType=None
)->list:
Apply a table of fix rows (chapter, verse, kind, read, printed, why) to assembled chapters; a chapter of None means every chapter with that verse.



V = lambda n, t, pg=1: dict(n=n, text=t, page=pg, heading=None)
_ch = lambda: [dict(heading='h1', colophon='c1', verses=[V(1, 'रामः गच्छति ॥१॥'), V(2, 'सीता ॥२॥'), V(4, 'क\nख\nग ॥४॥'), V(5, 'घ ॥५॥')]), dict(heading='h2', colophon='c2', verses=[V(1, 'रामः ॥१॥')])]
_p = []
_c = fix_chapters(_ch(), [(1, 1, 'fix', 'गच्छति', 'गच्छत्', 'typed'), (None, 1, 'fix', 'रामः', 'राम', ''), (1, 3, 'missing', None, 'लक्ष्मणः ॥३॥', 'from the 1905 print'),
                          (1, 5, 'recut', None, 2, ''), (1, 2, 'slip', 'सीता', None, 'so printed'), (2, 9, 'fix', 'x', 'y', ''), (1, 1, 'note', None, None, 'a lacuna'),
                          (1, 4, 'start', None, None, 'a leaf lost'), (2, 5, 'drop', None, None, 'a quotation')], _p)
test_eq([(c['heading'], c['colophon'], [(v['n'], v['text']) for v in c['verses']]) for c in _c],
        [('h1', None, [(1, 'राम गच्छत् ॥१॥'), (2, 'सीता ॥२॥'), (3, 'लक्ष्मणः ॥३॥')]), (None, 'c1', [(4, 'क\nख')]), ('h2', 'c2', [(1, 'राम ॥१॥')])])
test_eq(_p[:3], ['1.1 (1): read `गच्छति`, printed `गच्छत्` (typed)', '1.1 (1): read `रामः`, printed `राम`', '2.1 (1): read `रामः`, printed `राम`'])
test_eq(len(_p), 10); assert '2.9: verse 9 is gone from the reading; fix x → y not applied' in _p
test_eq([v['n'] for v in fix_chapters(_ch(), [((1, 'x'), 2, 'drop', None, None, '')], key=lambda i, c: (i, 'x'))[0]['verses']], [1, 4, 5])
test_fail(lambda: fix_chapters(_ch(), [(1, 1, 'mend', 'a', 'b', '')]))
_p = []; _c = fix_chapters([dict(heading=None, colophon=None, verses=[V(1, 'क क ॥१॥')])], [(1, 1, 'fix_all', 'क', 'ग', 'twice')], _p)
test_eq((_c[0]['verses'][0]['text'], _p), ('ग ग ॥१॥', ['1.1 (1): read `क`, printed `ग`, 2 times (twice)']))
_two = lambda: [dict(heading='h7', colophon='c8', verses=[V(1, 'a'), V(2, 'b'), V(25, 'y', 'p0107a'), V(2, 'z', 'p0108a'), V(3, 'w', 'p0108a')])]
_p = []; _c = fix_chapters(_two(), [(None, 2, 'start', None, 'p0108a', 'the leaf before it lost')], _p)   # two verses 2 in one chapter: the page picks
test_eq([[v['n'] for v in c['verses']] for c in _c], [[1, 2, 25], [2, 3]]); test_eq(_p, ['p0108a: a chapter starts at verse 2 (the leaf before it lost)'])
test_eq([[v['n'] for v in c['verses']] for c in fix_chapters(_two(), [(1, 2, 'start', None, 2, '')])], [[1, 2, 25], [2, 3]])   # or which one, from 1
test_eq([[v['n'] for v in c['verses']] for c in fix_chapters(_two(), [(1, 2, 'start', None, None, '')])], [[1], [2, 25, 2, 3]])   # else the first
_p = []; fix_chapters(_two(), [(1, 2, 'start', None, 'p0999a', '')], _p); test_eq(_p, ['1.2: no verse 2 after the first of a chapter (p0999a); the start not applied'])
_p = []
test_eq(sutras([dict(verses=[V(1, 'अथातो धर्म-\nजिज्ञासा ।'), V(2, 'चोदनालक्षणोऽर्थो धर्मः ॥')])], _p)[0]['verses'][0]['text'], 'अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा ॥'); test_eq(_p, ['1.1 (1): closing ॥ supplied'])

title: verses
text:
A vision model reads each page of a book and returns a list of blocks. A block is one piece of the page as the model saw it: a verse, a chapter heading, a commentary, a colophon (the line that closes a chapter, इति … अध्यायः), or a stretch of prose. Each block has a kind that says which of these it is, the printed number n if it has one, and its text. A page is a dict {page, blocks}, which is what vishalakshi.read_doc returns.
Readers do not all use the same names. vedicreader’s saved readings keep a page’s blocks under items instead of blocks, and some models call a heading head. blocks returns a page’s blocks under either key, and kind returns a block’s kind with head read as heading, through the KINDS table.
The functions in this module put verses into chapters. A verse comes out as {n, text, page, heading}: its number, its text, the page it was printed on, and the heading printed just before it, if any. Whenever a function changes a number or a text, it adds a line to probs, a list you pass in, so that a proofreader can check each change against the scan.

blocks
def blocks(
    p
)->list:
A page’s list of blocks, whether the page keeps them under blocks or under items.
source

kind
def kind(
    b
)->str | None:
A block’s kind, with an alias from KINDS, such as head, read as the kind it stands for.
test_eq(blocks(dict(page=1, items=[1])), [1]); test_eq(blocks(dict(page=1, blocks=[2], items=[1])), [2]); test_eq(blocks(dict(page=1)), [])
test_eq(kind(dict(kind='head')), 'heading'); test_eq(kind(dict(kind='verse')), 'verse'); test_eq(kind({}), None)

title: verses
text:
Verse numbers
A verse number can be printed in ASCII, Devanagari or Tamil digits, and is often wrapped in daṇḍas or brackets, as in ॥ २६ ॥ or (௪௦). vnum finds the digits and returns the number as an int, or None when there are no digits. Older Tamil prints write numbers with the signs ௰ (ten), ௱ (hundred) and ௲ (thousand), and vnum reads those too: ௬௱௨ is 602.
Sometimes a block carries two numbers, as in २६॥२७. This usually means the model read two verses as one block, so vnum returns the last number, 27. If you pass probs, it also records that verses 26 and 27 were printed as one. Some books print a running number followed by the verse’s number within its section, as in २६॥ १. For those, pick='first' returns the running number. The tests below show each case.


source

vnum
def vnum(
    n, page:NoneType=None, probs:list=None, pick:str='last'
)->int | None:
A printed verse number as an int, or None when it has no digits; when several are printed together, the last one, or the first with pick='first'.



_p = []
test_eq(vnum('॥ २६ ॥'), 26); test_eq(vnum('(௪௦)'), 40); test_eq(vnum(12), 12); test_eq(vnum(None), None)
test_eq(vnum('२६॥२७', 'p5', _p), 27); test_eq(_p, ['p5: verses 26-27 printed as one, numbered 27'])
test_eq(vnum('௬௱௨'), 602); test_eq(vnum('௨௱௩'), 203); test_eq(vnum('௰'), 10)
test_eq(vnum('२६॥ १', pick='first'), 26)   # a running number, then the count within its part

title: verses
text:
Mending a run
Within a chapter the numbers should run 1, 2, 3 without gaps. Two common mistakes break that run in a way the neighbouring numbers can repair, and mend repairs both.
The first is a number read twice. If the model reads 148, 150, 150, 151, the verse after 148 has to be 149, so mend takes the first 150 as 149. The second is two verses read as one block. If the model reads verse 148 and then a long block numbered 150, verse 149 is missing and is probably the first half of that block. mend splits the block after its last inner line that ends with a daṇḍa (।, ॥ or |) or a full stop, keeping at least three lines in the first part, and numbers that part 149. Both repairs happen only when the verse before is numbered exactly two less.
That rule suits verses printed on four lines. In a book of two-line verses, both lines of a verse end in a daṇḍa, so the last such line is the wrong place to cut. pair=True lets the first part be two lines long and cuts where the two parts come out closest in length.
renumber repairs the mistakes found in long chapters. One is a run read at a constant offset: in 52, 63, 64, 65, 56 the model misread the tens digit of three verses, and the sequence returns to normal at 56. Another is a single number that disagrees with both neighbours, such as 9 between 2 and 4, or a number that lost its leading digit, such as 1 read for 101 between 100 and 102. renumber only changes numbered verses. A verse with no number stays where it is.


source

renumber
def renumber(
    vs, where, probs:list
)->list:
Correct misread verse numbers in a chapter from the numbers around them, leaving unnumbered verses where they are.




source

mend
def mend(
    vs, probs:list, pair:bool=False
)->list:
Correct a verse number read twice and split two verses read as one block, where the numbers around them show what is right.



V = lambda n, t='a ।\nb ॥', pg=1: dict(n=n, text=t, page=pg, heading=None)
_p = []
test_eq([v['n'] for v in mend([V(148), V(150), V(150), V(151)], _p)], [148, 149, 150, 151]); test_eq(len(_p), 1)
_p = []
_m = mend([V(1), V(3, 'a\nb\nc ॥\nd\ne ॥')], _p)
test_eq([(v['n'], v['text']) for v in _m], [(1, 'a ।\nb ॥'), (2, 'a\nb\nc ॥'), (3, 'd\ne ॥')])
_p = []
test_eq([v['n'] for v in renumber([V(n) for n in (52, 63, 64, 65, 56, 57)], 'ch 3', _p)], [52, 53, 54, 55, 56, 57]); test_eq(len(_p), 3)
test_eq([v['n'] for v in renumber([V(n) for n in (99, 100, 1, 102)], 'ch 9', [])], [99, 100, 101, 102])
test_eq([v['n'] for v in renumber([V(None), V(99), V(100), V(1), V(102)], 'ch 9', [])], [None, 99, 100, 101, 102])   # an unnumbered opener stays put
test_eq([v['n'] for v in mend([V(None), V(1), V(3, 'a\nb\nc ॥\nd\ne ॥')], [])], [None, 1, 2, 3])

title: verses
text:
Chapters
assemble reads the pages in order and builds chapters, each a dict {heading, colophon, verses}. It returns the chapters and a list of problems.
The kinds argument says which blocks count as verse. By default these are blocks of kind verse and blocks with no kind. With kinds=None, every block except headings and colophons counts as verse, which suits a reading in which the model gave verse text kind names of its own.
A heading becomes the name of the open chapter if that chapter has no name yet, or opens a new chapter if none is open. Each verse also keeps the heading printed just before it in its own heading field. A verse numbered 1 after a higher number starts a new chapter. A colophon ends the open chapter and is stored as its colophon.
A verse that starts at the foot of one page often has its number printed only at its end, on the next page, so the model returns the first part as a block with no number. assemble holds every unnumbered block and adds its text to the next numbered verse. If a colophon comes while text is still held, that text becomes the chapter’s last verse, numbered one more than the verse before it, and this is recorded in the problems.
A book photographed as two-page spreads may show the same page twice, and then the model reads the same verse twice. A numbered verse whose number and last line match a verse already in the chapter is dropped, and an unnumbered block that repeats the one held before it is kept once. As verses are added, any break in the numbering, such as verse 5 after verse 3, is listed in the problems. When every page is in, mend runs on each chapter.
Many books print a commentary after each verse; in Tamil books this is the urai. The model gives such a block a kind of its own, such as urai, gloss or bhashya. Name those kinds in notes, and assemble keeps each such block with the verse it follows, in verse['notes'][kind], as a list of texts. A commentary that arrives while verse text is still held, with no number yet, is kept for the next verse that is added. With the default kinds and no notes, these blocks are skipped. Some books, the Vidhānamālai among them, print the number at the end of the commentary and leave the verse unnumbered. With number_from_note=True, a numbered commentary block gives its number to the verse text held before it, and this is recorded in the problems.
A page break can also cut a block in two, so that its second half opens the next page. Some readings mark that second half with cont. Only when you pass cont=True does assemble first join each such half to the block it continues, using join_cont on a copy of the pages.
Not every unnumbered block belongs to the next verse. Many books open with a maṅgala, a verse of blessing printed before verse 1 without a number, and commentaries quote whole verses from other works. Such a block ends in ॥ like a finished verse. By default assemble treats it like any other unnumbered block and adds its text to the next numbered verse, which then holds two verses. With openers=True, an unnumbered block that ends in ॥ is kept as a verse of its own, with n set to None. It goes into the chapter of the numbered verse that follows it, just before that verse; if a colophon comes first, it goes at the end of the chapter the colophon closes. mend and renumber leave such verses where they are.
join_cont is the joining step on its own. When the first block on a page is marked cont and has the same kind as the last block on the page before, its text is added to that block: after a line break for a verse, and after a space for anything else. If the earlier text ends in a hyphen, the hyphen is removed and the two parts are joined with no space, so a word split across the page break is whole again. If the second half carries a number, the joined block takes it. join_cont changes the pages it is given and returns them.

title: verses
text:
Chapters cut at their colophons
Some editions print no usable chapter headings and number each chapter only in its colophon. The Khemraj edition of the Bṛhat Parāśara Horā Śāstra is one. It has a pūrva khaṇḍa (first part) of 51 adhyāyas (chapters) and an uttara bhāga (second part) of 20, and a chapter’s number appears only in its closing line, such as इति … राशिभेदनामाध्यायः ॥ ३ ॥. assemble_colophon cuts the pages into chapters at these colophons. Each chapter comes out as {part, no, name, heading, colophon, verses}. By default every block other than a heading or a colophon counts as verse (kinds=None).
A colophon closes a chapter only if it contains adh, which is ध्याय by default, as in अध्यायः. The chapter’s number is the first number after the last adh in the colophon. Failing that, it is the colophon block’s own n, and failing that, one more than the previous chapter in the same part. The chapter’s name is the text after one of the anchor words, such as जातके or होरायां, and before नाम, or before the ordinal word and अध्याय. If the colophon gives no name, the chapter takes one from an earlier heading of the form अथ … अध्यायः.
parts lists the book’s parts in order, each with a pattern. The pages start in the first part, and a heading or colophon that matches a later part’s pattern moves the count into that part, so chapter numbers can start again at 1 in the uttara bhāga.
These editions also print things that are not the text, and there is a pattern for each. A colophon matching contents closes a table of contents printed before the text, so everything collected up to it is thrown away. A heading matching skip starts the commentator’s own verses, such as his maṅgala or his praise of the author, and verses are skipped until a heading matching resume. Commentators also write colophons of their own. A colophon matching tika (टीका or व्याख्या) that repeats the number of the chapter just closed marks the verses between the two colophons as commentary, and they are dropped. An ordinary colophon that repeats the number adds those verses to that chapter instead.
If the verses before a colophon start again at 1 partway through, the chapter before them lost its colophon. The function then splits the verses where the numbering restarts, giving the first part the number before and no colophon or name, unless a chapter with that number already exists. Unnumbered blocks are held and joined to the next numbered verse, and repeated verses are dropped, as in assemble. With pair=True, text still held when a colophon arrives becomes the chapter’s last verse, and mend uses its rule for two-line verses. Finally each chapter goes through renumber and mend, and any break left in its numbering is listed in the problems.
The test below runs a small two-page book through these cases.

text:
Typing slips
Three small helpers fix slips in Devanagari typed by a person or written by a model.
norm turns a colon written after a Devanagari letter into a visarga (ः), writes ASCII digits between ॥ marks in Devanagari digits, and removes spaces before a daṇḍa (। or ॥). So राम: ॥ 1 ॥ becomes रामः॥ १॥.
A pāda is a quarter of a verse, usually printed as a line or half line ending in a daṇḍa. A word at the end of a pāda often ends in a bare consonant marked with a virāma, as in जगत्, and typists drop the virāma. virama puts it back when a line ends with one of a few endings that need it, either at the end of the line or before a ।. The endings are त after ा, े, ृ, व or य (-ात्, -ेत्, -ृत्, -वत्, -यत्), न after ा or ि (-ान्, -िन्), and the whole words जगत and सत. A word before ॥ is not changed.
deva writes a number in Devanagari digits.

title: book
text:
read_book takes a PDF or a page image of a book of verses and does the whole job. It sends every page to the vision model model through vishalakshi’s read_doc, with the reading prompt named by preset (sanskrit by default) and any hint you add, such as “Each verse ends in ॥ n ॥.”. The model returns each page as a list of blocks, the pieces it found on the page: verses with their printed numbers, headings, colophons (the line that closes a chapter, इति … अध्यायः) and prose. read_book then passes the pages to assemble_book, described below.
If you pass a vishalakshi vault, the pages are stored there as versions of one document, and the result’s doc_id names it. Without a vault nothing is stored and doc_id is None. Other keyword arguments go on to read_doc. The most useful is cache, a folder where each page’s reading is saved as JSON, so that reading the book a second time sends nothing to the model. tries, progress, spread, strips and the rest work as they do in read_doc. chat replaces the model with a function of your own, which is how the tests below run without one.
The result holds the chapters, the probs, the prose blocks left out of the verses, the number of pages, the cost of the reading, and the pages vishalakshi reports as failed, unread or blocked. probs is a list of lines, one for every change lekhaka made and every place a proofreader should look at the scan.
assemble_book is the second half on its own, for pages that have already been read. A common case is a vault whose pages other models have proofread, with the corrections accepted: you take the pages back out of the vault and assemble them again. It works in this order:

A verse block read without a number takes the number its text ends on, if that is a number between ॥ marks (॥ १२ ॥). Blocks with no text are removed, except table blocks, which carry rows.
fixes, a table of fix rows for apply_fixes (see repairs), is applied.
With cont=True, blocks that a page break cut in two are joined (join_cont).
assemble builds the chapters, with pair, kinds, notes, number_from_note and openers passed to it.
With renumber=True, each chapter goes through renumber.
When fix is on, as it is by default, and script is Devanagari, each verse with malformed akṣaras (syllables written in a form no printer would set) is repaired with fix_aksharas, and the repair is listed in probs.
If you give counts, the number of verses expected in each chapter, every chapter with a different number is listed in probs.

The prose blocks, which are not verse, come back in left. read_book takes the same options except cont, which only assemble_book has.
book_md writes chapters out as markdown: a heading for each chapter, each verse followed by its number in italics, and the colophon at the end.

_v.proofread(_cb.doc_id, ['a', 'b'], pages=[1], chats=dict(a=Says('ग ॥२॥'), b=Says('ग ॥२॥')))
_v.accept(_cb.doc_id)
_ab = assemble_book([dict(page=p.page, blocks=p.blocks) for p in _v.pages(_cb.doc_id)])
test_eq([(v['n'], v['text']) for v in _ab.chapters[0]['verses']], [(1, 'क ॥१॥'), (2, 'ग ॥२॥')])
# a verse read without its number takes the one it closes on; a maṅgala kept with `openers`; renumbered; the prose left out
_ps = [dict(page=1, blocks=[dict(kind='verse', text='श्रीगणेशाय नमः ॥'), dict(kind='verse', text='धर्मो रक्षति ॥ ௧ ॥'), dict(kind='prose', text='टीका'),
                            dict(kind='verse', text=''), dict(kind='verse', text='सत्यं वद ॥ ३ ॥')])]
_ab = assemble_book(_ps, kinds=('verse',), openers=True, renumber=True)
test_eq([v['n'] for v in _ab.chapters[0]['verses']], [None, 1, 3])   # ௧ read as 1; the gap is the print's, noted
test_eq([b['text'] for b in _ab.left], ['टीका']); assert any('3' in x for x in _ab.probs), _ab.probs

title: lekhaka
text:
lekhaka (लेखक, “scribe”) takes a printed book of verses, such as a Sanskrit or Tamil text, and gives back its chapters with every verse numbered.
A vision model reads each page through vishalakshi and returns it as a list of blocks. A block is one piece of the page: a verse with its printed number, a chapter heading, a commentary, or a colophon, the line that closes a chapter (इति … अध्यायः). Models make mistakes on old prints. They miss a verse number, read two verses as one block, or lose half a verse at a page break. They also write Devanagari no printer would set. lekhaka finds and fixes these slips, puts the verses into chapters, and lists every change it made so that a person can check it against the scan.

title: lekhaka
text:
Install
pip install lekhaka

title: lekhaka
text:
How to use
from lekhaka import read_book, book_md
from vishalakshi import Vault

b = read_book('gita.pdf', Vault('books.db'), model='claude/sonnet', title='Bhagavad Gita',
              hint='Each verse ends in ॥ n ॥.', counts=[47, 72])
b.chapters[0]['verses'][:2]     # [{n, text, page, heading}, ...]
b.probs                         # what was changed or needs checking, page by page
print(book_md(b.chapters, 'Bhagavad Gita'))
counts is the number of verses you expect in each chapter, usually from the book’s table of contents. lekhaka reports any chapter that comes out with a different number.
If you pass a vault, each page is stored as a version of one document. You can then have other models read the pages again with vault.proofread(b.doc_id, readers), and apply the corrections you agree with using vault.accept. Without a vault, nothing is stored.
Each function also works on its own. The input is a list of pages, each {page, blocks}, which is what vishalakshi.read_doc returns. The rest of this page runs every public function on real pages.

The samples
nbs/samples holds pages from three books that vedicreader has read, saved exactly as the model returned them.

import json
from copy import deepcopy


bj, vm, uro = [json.load(open(f'samples/{k}.json')) for k in ('brihat_jataka', 'vidhanamalai', 'uromarishi')]
len(bj), len(vm), len(uro)

title: lekhaka
text:
verses
Models do not label blocks consistently. One calls a heading head and another heading; vedicreader stores a page’s blocks under items and vishalakshi under blocks. kind and blocks accept both.
vnum reads a printed verse number in any digits, Devanagari, Tamil or ASCII. The first verse on this Pañcapakṣi page is numbered 205 in Tamil numerals. Some books print two numbers on a verse, such as २६॥२७; vnum takes the last unless you ask for the first.

kind(dict(kind='head')), len(blocks(uro[0])), vnum(uro[0]['blocks'][1]['n']), vnum('२६॥२७'), vnum('२६॥ १', pick='first')

('heading', 8, 205, 27, 26)


assemble puts the verses into chapters. A colophon closes the current chapter, and a chapter also ends when the numbering drops back to 1. A heading names the chapter it falls in, if that chapter has no name yet; it does not start a chapter by itself. A block with no number is taken to be the start of the next numbered verse, because a verse that begins at the foot of one page often gets its number only on the next. The sixteen Bṛhajjātaka pages give two chapters, of 8 and 22 verses, with nothing to report:

chs, probs = assemble(bj)
[(c['heading'], len(c['verses']), c['colophon'][:30]) for c in chs], probs

([('वियोनिजन्माध्यायः', 8, 'इति श्रीवराहमिहिरकृते बृहज्जात'),
  ('निषेकाध्यायः', 22, 'इति श्रीवराहमिहिरकृते बृहज्जात')],
 [])


Some blocks without a number are whole verses, not pieces of one. A book may open with a maṅgala, a verse of blessing printed before verse 1, and a commentary may quote a verse from another work. Such a block ends in ॥ like any verse but carries no number, and adding it to the next verse is wrong.
Page p0025a of the Bṛhajjātaka has one. Between verses 3 and 4 the commentary quotes a verse in the āryā metre. By default assemble adds it to verse 4, which ends up with four lines instead of two. With openers=True, a block that ends in ॥ and has no number stays a separate verse, with n set to None:

op, _ = assemble(bj, openers=True)
[(v['n'], v['page'], v['text'][:25]) for v in op[1]['verses'][2:5]], len(chs[1]['verses'][3]['text'].split('\n'))

([(3, 'p0025a', 'रवीन्दुशुक्रावनिजैः स्वभा'),
  (None, 'p0025a', 'बलयुतौ स्वगृहांशेष्वर्कसि'),
  (4, 'p0025a', 'दिवाकरेन्द्वोः स्मरगौ कुज')],
 4)


Many books print a commentary under each verse. notes=('urai',) keeps blocks of that kind with the verse they explain, in verse['notes'], instead of counting them as verse text. Some books number the commentary and leave the verse unnumbered, and the Vidhānamālai is one of them. number_from_note=True gives each verse the number of its commentary.
join_cont joins a block that a page break cut in two. The model marks the second half with cont, and a word hyphenated across the break is put back together. assemble(cont=True) does this before anything else.

vc, _ = assemble(vm, notes=('urai',), number_from_note=True)
v = vc[0]['verses'][0]
len(vc[0]['verses']), v['n'], v['notes']['urai'][0][:40]

(11, 1, '(என்றது.) ஸ்ரீமகாலக்ஷ்மிக்கு நாயகரும், ப')



join_cont([dict(page=1, blocks=[dict(kind='prose', text='a com-')]), dict(page=2, blocks=[dict(kind='prose', text='mentary', cont=True)])])[0]['blocks'][0]['text']

'a commentary'


mend fixes two common slips in a chapter’s numbering. When the model reads the same number twice, as in 7, 9, 9, 10, it takes the first 9 as 8. When the model reads two verses as one block, it splits them. renumber fixes a run of numbers that are wrong the same way: in 52, 63, 64, 65, 56 the model misread the tens digit three times. check_counts compares each chapter’s number of verses with the count you expect:

V = lambda n: dict(n=n, text='a ।\nb ॥', page='p1')
p = []; [v['n'] for v in mend([V(7), V(9), V(9), V(10)], p)], p

([7, 8, 9, 10], ['p1: first of two 9s taken as 8'])



[v['n'] for v in renumber([V(n) for n in (52, 63, 64, 65, 56)], 'ch 3', [])], check_counts(chs, [8, 21])

([52, 53, 54, 55, 56], ['chapter 2: 22 verses, the plan has 21'])


Some books print no chapter headings, and the only marker is the colophon at the end of each chapter, such as इति श्रीवराहमिहिरकृते बृहज्जातके निषेकाध्यायश्चतुर्थः. assemble_colophon starts a new chapter after each colophon and reads the chapter’s part, number and name from it. It ignores colophons that belong to a commentary.

cc, _ = assemble_colophon(bj)
[(c['part'], c['no'], c['name'], len(c['verses'])) for c in cc]

[('पूर्व', 3, 'वियोनिजन्म', 8), ('पूर्व', 4, 'निषेक', 22)]


Models sometimes write akṣaras that cannot occur, such as a virāma followed by a vowel sign (ध्ा). bad_aksharas names each fault and fix_aksharas repairs it. Three smaller helpers deal with typing slips: deva writes a number in Devanagari digits, norm replaces a colon used for a visarga and ASCII digits inside ॥ ॥, and virama puts back a virāma dropped at the end of a pāda.

bad_aksharas('ध्ार्म'), fix_aksharas('ध्ार्म'), deva(18), norm('राम: ॥ 1 ॥'), virama('जगत ।')

(['virāma before a vowel sign'], 'धार्म', '१८', 'रामः॥ १॥', 'जगत् ।')

title: lekhaka
text:
book
read_book does the whole job for a PDF. It reads the pages through vishalakshi and passes them to assemble_book, which applies your fix rows, gives a verse read without its number the number it ends on (॥ १२ ॥), assembles the chapters, repairs akṣaras, and compares the chapters with counts. read_book takes renumber=True to renumber each chapter. Joining blocks split by a page break (cont=True) is an option of assemble_book only, for pages you already have. book_md writes chapters as markdown:

print(book_md(chs[:1], 'बृहज्जातकम्')[:160])

title: lekhaka
text:
repairs
Some mistakes need a person. You look at the scan, decide what the page really says, and write that down as a row. lekhaka applies the rows and records each change in probs, so the list of problems also says what was changed and why.
apply_fixes works on pages, before assemble. A row is (page, block, kind, read, printed, why): the text the model read, the text the page prints, and your reason. A fix row replaces the first match and a fix_all row replaces every match.

apply_fixes(deepcopy(bj), [('p0022b', 2, 'fix', 'शेभनाः', 'शोभनाः', 'a typo')], probs=(p := [])); p

['p0022b: read `शेभनाः`, printed `शोभनाः` (a typo)']


number_runs numbers verses printed without numbers when they sit between two numbered verses, since the gap says what the missing numbers must be. borrow_numbers takes a missing number from a second reading of the same page, when both readings have the same verse.

number_runs([dict(page='p1', blocks=[dict(kind='verse', n=1, text='a'), dict(kind='verse', text='b'), dict(kind='verse', n=3, text='c')])], p := [])
mine = deepcopy(bj[:1]); mine[0]['blocks'][2]['n'] = None
borrow_numbers(mine, bj, p); p

['p1: verse printed without its number taken as 2, between 1 and 3',
 "p0022b: verse 2's number, lost in this reading, taken from the other (1.00)"]


cut_by_plan starts a chapter where you say one starts, given as (page, where, why), where where is a block’s position on the page or the first words of a heading. Use it when a book prints neither a heading nor a colophon that assemble can find. drop_pages removes the verses on pages that are not part of the text, such as a preface or an index.

cut_by_plan(deepcopy(vm), [('p0020a', 'பதிகம்.', 'the contents open a chapter')], p := [])
drop_pages(deepcopy(bj), [('p0029b', 'p0030a')], p); p

['p0020a: a chapter starts at `பதிகம்.`, by the plan (the contents open a chapter)',
 'p0029b: verses dropped, not the text',
 'p0030a: verses dropped, not the text']


fix_chapters works on chapters, after assemble, and finds a verse by its chapter and number instead of its page and position. Its rows are (chapter, verse, kind, read, printed, why). Besides fix and fix_all, a note row records a remark without changing the text, and a start row starts a new chapter at a verse.
If a chapter holds two verses with the same number, a start row’s printed says which one is meant: the page it is on, or 1 for the first and 2 for the second.

rows = [(1, 2, 'fix', 'शेभनाः', 'शोभनाः', 'a typo'), (2, 19, 'fix_all', '।।', '॥', 'doubled daṇḍas'), (2, 15, 'note', None, None, 'its first two lines are a quotation')]
fix_chapters(deepcopy(chs), rows, p := []); p

['1.2 (p0022b): read `शेभनाः`, printed `शोभनाः` (a typo)',
 '2.19 (p0029a): read `।।`, printed `॥`, 2 times (doubled daṇḍas)',
 '2.15: its first two lines are a quotation']



one = [dict(heading=None, colophon=None, verses=chs[0]['verses'] + chs[1]['verses'])]
p = []; [len(c['verses']) for c in fix_chapters(one, [(1, 1, 'start', None, 'p0024b', 'by hand')], p)], p

([8, 22], ['p0024b: a chapter starts at verse 1.1 (by hand)'])


Works in sūtra form need different handling. sutras joins each sūtra onto one line and closes it with ॥.

sutras([dict(verses=[dict(n=1, text='अथातो धर्म-\nजिज्ञासा ।', page='p1')])], p := [])[0]['verses'][0]['text'], p

('अथातो धर्मजिज्ञासा ॥', ['1.1 (p1): closing ॥ supplied'])

title: lekhaka
text:
editions
vedicreader publishes a work as a set of titles. cut divides chapters into titles: one per chapter, one every per verses, or the whole work as one. A verse without a number, such as the quoted āryā above, gets a letter (क, ख and so on) in place of a number, with the word open_word (मङ्गलम्) as its label.
numbering summarises a run of verses: how many are numbered, which numbers are skipped or repeated, and the first and last.

[t['title'] for t in cut(cc, 'chapters', book='बृहज्जातकम्')], [(v['n'], v.get('word')) for v in cut(op, 'chapters')[1]['verses'][2:5]]

(['बृहज्जातकम् १ वियोनिजन्म', 'बृहज्जातकम् २ निषेक'],
 [(3, None), ('क', 'मङ्गलम्'), (4, None)])



numbering(op[1]['verses'])

{'numbered': 22,
 'unnumbered': 1,
 'skipped': [],
 'repeated': [],
 'first': 1,
 'last': 22}


The next functions compare a reading with another edition of the same text, called a witness. witness_verses takes the raw HTML of a witness page, from GRETIL for example, and returns its numbered verses. letters reduces a verse to its letters, dropping numbers, punctuation and bracketed notes, so that two editions can be compared on the words alone. text_changes proposes a change wherever the closest verse in the witness spells a word differently, and also flags dropped virāmas.

witness_verses('<p>क ख ॥ १ ॥</p><p>ग घ ॥ २ ॥</p>'), letters('रामः ॥ १ ॥ (टि)')

([(1, 'क ख'), (2, 'ग घ')], 'रामः')



wit = [(v['n'], v['text'].replace('शेभनाः', 'शोभनाः')) for v in chs[0]['verses']]
[(c['id'], c['read'], c['print'], c['why']) for c in text_changes(chs[:1], wit)]

[('1.2.w4', 'शेभनाः', 'शोभनाः', 'the witness (2) reads so')]


ref_check flags verses that read very differently from a reference edition, which usually means a misread or a lost line. move_lines fixes a common slip, where the last line of one verse was read as the first line of the next, by moving the line back.

ref = {1: [letters(v['text']) for v in chs[0]['verses']]}; ref[1][4] = ''
ref_check(chs[:1], ref)

['1.5 (p0023a): reads unlike the reference (0.29), check against the scan']



mv = deepcopy(chs[:1]); a, b = mv[0]['verses'][:2]; ls = a['text'].split('\n')
a['text'], b['text'] = ls[0], ls[1] + '\n' + b['text']
move_lines(mv, {(1, v['n']): letters(v['text']) for v in chs[0]['verses']}, p := []); p, mv[0]['verses'][0]['text'] == chs[0]['verses'][0]['text']

(['1.2: 1 leading line(s) moved back to 1.1'], True)


The last group measures how far apart two readings of the same pages are, which is useful when you try a second model. verse_text collects a page’s verse text, lev is the edit distance between two strings, and disagree is the share of a page’s text that differs. compare puts the result for each page in a table and summarises it. Here the second reading lost the first verse on p0023a, and that page stands out:

b2 = deepcopy(bj); b2[1]['blocks'] = b2[1]['blocks'][1:]   # a second reading that lost p0023a's first verse
verse_text(bj[1])[:12], lev('क्रियः', 'क्रिया'), round(disagree(bj[1], b2[1]), 2)

('क्रियःशिरोवक', 1, 0.34)



md, flag = compare({'opus': bj, 'other': b2}, [('opus', 'other')])
print(md)

| page | opus vs other |
|---|---|
| p0023a | 34.1% |

opus vs other: 16 pages, mean 2.1%, 1 at 10% or more

title: editions
text: These functions work on the chapters assemble returns, [{heading, colophon, verses}], where a colophon is the line that closes a chapter. A few work on a single page of blocks, the pieces of a page a vision model returns: verses, headings, colophons, commentary and prose. Several compare a reading with another edition of the same work, called a witness. You fetch or load the witness yourself and pass it in; nothing here reads a file or goes to the web.

title: editions
text:
Titles
vedicreader publishes a work as a set of titles, each a page of verses with its own name. cut divides chapters into titles, each {name, title, chapter, verses}, in one of three ways chosen by how:

how='per', the default, makes one title for every per verses (10 by default) across the whole work, by the verses’ own numbers: verses 1 to 10, then 11 to 20, and so on. An unnumbered verse goes with the numbered verse before it, and unnumbered verses before the first numbered one go with the first title. A title’s range stops at the last number it actually holds, and every title has chapter 1.
how='chapters' makes one title for each chapter, named from book, the chapter’s number and its heading.
how='one' puts the whole work in a single title.

name is a file name built from stem, such as work_011_012 or work_02, and title is the heading a reader sees, with its numbers written by digits (Devanagari by default).
A verse with no number, such as a maṅgala (a verse of blessing that opens a book) or a verse a commentary quotes, still needs a label. cut gives it a letter, क, ख, ग and so on, starting again from क after each numbered verse, and sets its word to open_word (मङ्गलम् by default). An unnumbered verse therefore never takes a number that belongs to a numbered verse.
numbering reports what a run of verses’ own numbers say: how many verses are numbered and unnumbered, which numbers are skipped or repeated, and the first and last.

Divide chapters’ verses into titles [{name, title, chapter, verses}]: one for every per verses, one for each chapter, or one for the whole work.



V = lambda n, t='x': dict(n=n, text=t, page=1, heading=None)
_cs = [dict(heading='प्रथमः', verses=[V(None), V(None), V('१'), V(2)]), dict(heading='द्वितीयः', verses=[V(3), V(None), V('௧௧'), V(12)])]

        [('work_001_003', 'शतकम् १–३', ['क', 'ख', 1, 2, 3, 'क']), ('work_011_012', 'शतकम् ११–१२', [11, 12])])
test_eq(cut(_cs)[0]['verses'][0]['word'], 'मङ्गलम्'); test_eq('word' in cut(_cs)[0]['verses'][2], False)
test_eq([(t['name'], t['title']) for t in cut(_cs, 'chapters', stem='s', book='ग्रन्थः')], [('s_01', 'ग्रन्थः १ प्रथमः'), ('s_02', 'ग्रन्थः २ द्वितीयः')])
test_eq(len(cut(_cs, 'one')[0]['verses']), 8)
test_eq(numbering([V(1), V(None), V('३'), V('௩'), V(6)]), dict(numbered=4, unnumbered=1, skipped=[2, 4, 5], repeated=[3], first=1, last=6))

title: editions
text:
A witness
A witness is another edition of the same text, used to check a reading. It might be a page from sanskritdocuments.org or a GRETIL file. witness_verses takes the raw page, HTML or plain text, removes the markup, and cuts it into verses at each verse number written as ॥ n ॥ or || n ||, returning [(n, text)]. GRETIL writes each number with a reference, as in || BharSt_1.12 ||, and the verse number is taken from its end. Only the last six lines before each number are kept, so a page header does not end up in the first verse. If the page is in IAST (Roman letters with diacritics) instead of Devanagari, pass a translit function; it is used when the page has fewer than 200 Devanagari characters. A witness shows where to look again; the reading should still follow the scan, not the witness.
Two editions differ in punctuation, numbering and notes even where their words agree. letters reduces a text to its Devanagari letters alone, removing the verse number between ॥ marks, bracketed notes, spaces, daṇḍas and digits. The checks below compare texts in this form.
text_changes proposes corrections and does not make them. It does two checks.

On each line it looks for a pāda-final virāma that was dropped, using virama. A pāda is a quarter of a verse, usually ending in a daṇḍa, and a virāma (्) is the mark that removes a consonant’s vowel. These changes have by set to ['rule'].
When you pass wit, the output of witness_verses, it finds the witness verse whose letters are most like the verse’s, if they are at least at alike (0.7 by default), and compares the two word by word. Where one or two words are spelled differently, it proposes the witness’s spelling, with by set to ['witness']. You can also pass metre, a function that takes a verse’s lines and returns the metre’s name if they scan, or None. A verse that already scans is not compared, and if a proposed change makes a verse scan, by also lists 'metre'.

Each change is a dict {id, chapter, n, page, read, print, why, by}. A proofreader accepts or rejects each one, and an accepted change can be applied as a fix row for fix_chapters, with its read and print as the read and printed text.

title: editions
text:
Against a reference edition
A reference edition is a complete text of the same work, close enough to compare whole verses with. For ref_check, ref is {chapter: [letters of each verse]}, built with letters as in the test below.
ref_check reports problems and changes nothing. It compares each verse with the reference verses near it, meaning within win (6) places of its position or of its number, and flags it when even the best match is less than at (0.8) alike. That usually means a misread or a lost line. It also flags a verse containing a lacuna mark (·· or …), where the print itself shows missing text. Verses past the end of a shorter reference are not checked.
The model sometimes puts the boundary between two verses in the wrong place, so that the last line of verse 4 is read as the first line of verse 5. move_lines repairs this by comparing with a reference given as {(chapter, n): text}, where each text has been reduced by fold (letters by default, or a function of your own for a reference in IAST). When a verse matches its reference much better without its first lines, move_lines does one of three things. If adding those lines to the verse before makes that verse match its own reference better, it moves them back. If the rest of the verse then matches closely and the lines match no reference verse from n-2 to n+2, they are taken as a quotation the editor printed, and dropped. Otherwise it changes nothing and asks for a check by hand. Each case is recorded in probs.
In both functions key(i, chapter) gives the name a chapter has in the reference; by default it is the chapter’s position counting from 1.

title: editions
text:
Two readings of a page
When you try a second model, or read a book again, you want to know where the two readings differ. These functions measure that page by page.
verse_text joins the text of a page’s verse blocks as bare letters, removing numbers, daṇḍas, spaces, punctuation and the avagraha (ऽ). With numbered=True it keeps only the verses read with a number, which leaves out the part of a verse carried over a page break and verses a commentary quotes. lev counts the character edits (insertions, deletions and substitutions) that turn one string into another. disagree is the share of a page’s text that differs between two readings: the edits divided by the length of the longer text. It is 1 when only one reading found any verse on the page, and None when neither did or one reading lacks the page.
compare takes named readings, each a list of pages or a dict from page name to page, and pairs of names to compare. It returns a markdown table and a list of flagged pages, the pages where the first pair differs by at (10%) or more. The table shows only the flagged pages, followed by one summary line per pair giving the number of pages, the mean difference and how many pages reach at. If you pass pages, the table shows exactly those pages instead.
